# Grade 11 Argumentative Essay Rubric
## Designed for Speed + Reliability (120 essays / weekend)

---

## Why This Design Works

Marking 120 essays reliably in a weekend (roughly 40/day, or one every 8–10 minutes if you work 6 hours/day) fails when rubrics have too many criteria, vague descriptors, or require the marker to "hold" a mental standard that drifts over time. This rubric solves that with:

- **4 criteria only** (not 6–8)
- **4 levels only** (not 5 or 7 — avoids false precision and endless hovering over borderline scores)
- **Single defining sentence per level** wherever possible, so you can pattern-match fast
- A **calibration + batching process** that prevents drift, which is the real enemy of reliability, not the rubric itself

---

## The Rubric

**Total: 20 marks** (4 criteria × 5 marks each) — scales easily to your school's required total.

### Criterion 1: Argument & Position (5 marks)
*Is there a clear stance, argued logically?*

| Level | Marks | Descriptor |
|---|---|---|
| 4 – Convincing | 5 | Clear, consistent position; reasons are logical and build on each other; counter-argument acknowledged or refuted. |
| 3 – Competent | 4 | Clear position; reasons are logical but may repeat or not build cumulatively; little/no counter-argument. |
| 2 – Basic | 2–3 | Position is present but drifts, contradicts itself, or is asserted without real reasoning. |
| 1 – Inadequate | 0–1 | No clear position, or the essay is not actually argumentative (e.g., pure narrative/description). |

### Criterion 2: Evidence & Development (5 marks)
*Are claims supported and developed, not just stated?*

| Level | Marks | Descriptor |
|---|---|---|
| 4 – Convincing | 5 | Each main point has specific, relevant support (example, statistic, scenario, reasoning chain) developed in 3+ sentences. |
| 3 – Competent | 4 | Points have some support but development is thin (1–2 sentences) or generic. |
| 2 – Basic | 2–3 | Points are mostly asserted with minimal or vague support ("this is bad for society"). |
| 1 – Inadequate | 0–1 | No real support; list of unexplained claims. |

### Criterion 3: Structure & Cohesion (5 marks)
*Does it flow as a unified essay?*

| Level | Marks | Descriptor |
|---|---|---|
| 4 – Convincing | 5 | Clear intro (with stance) and conclusion (not repetitive); paragraphs ordered logically; strong linking words used correctly. |
| 3 – Competent | 4 | Intro/conclusion present but mechanical; paragraphing mostly logical; some linking words. |
| 2 – Basic | 2–3 | Intro or conclusion weak/missing; paragraphs are a series of unconnected points. |
| 1 – Inadequate | 0–1 | No discernible structure; one long block or random order. |

### Criterion 4: Language & Register (5 marks)
*Is it written accurately in a suitable argumentative register?*

| Level | Marks | Descriptor |
|---|---|---|
| 4 – Convincing | 5 | Errors are rare and don't impede meaning; register is formal/persuasive; sentence variety. |
| 3 – Competent | 4 | Occasional errors, meaning always clear; register mostly appropriate; some sentence variety. |
| 2 – Basic | 2–3 | Frequent errors; meaning sometimes unclear; register slips into casual/spoken style. |
| 1 – Inadequate | 0–1 | Errors seriously impede meaning throughout. |

---

## The Marking Process (This Is What Actually Saves You)

The rubric only works if the *process* prevents drift and fatigue-driven inconsistency. Follow this sequence:

### Step 1: Calibration (30–40 minutes, before you start)
- Randomly pull **8 essays** spanning the range you expect (weak, average, strong).
- Mark them cold, without over-thinking.
- Lay them out in rank order. Ask: *does this order feel right?* Adjust.
- These 8 become your **anchor set** — physically keep them beside you all weekend. When unsure about a borderline essay, compare it directly to the nearest anchor essay, not to an abstract standard in your head. This is the single biggest reliability booster available to a solo marker.

### Step 2: Batch by criterion, not by essay (optional but powerful)
Instead of marking essay 1 fully, then essay 2 fully, etc.:
- Mark **all 120 essays on Criterion 1 only**, then all 120 on Criterion 2, etc.

Why this works: your eye calibrates to *one thing at a time* (e.g., "is there a position and is it argued logically?") and stays sharp for that dimension across the batch, rather than resetting your judgment 4 times per essay × 120 essays. It also stops your impression of language quality from unconsciously inflating/deflating your view of the argument quality (the "halo effect").

If this feels too mechanical for a first attempt, a hybrid works too: mark 2 criteria per pass (Argument+Evidence in pass 1, Structure+Language in pass 2).

### Step 3: Work in sessions of ~25 essays, not marathon blocks
- After every ~25 essays (roughly 1 batch-criterion or 45–60 min), stop for 5–10 minutes.
- Re-read one of your anchor essays before resuming. This resets your internal scale, which drifts silently after sustained marking (markers reliably get either stricter or more lenient over a session — re-anchoring corrects for both).

### Step 4: Flag, don't agonize
- Any essay where you hover between two levels for more than ~20 seconds: **write the mark you lean toward, flag it (star/sticky note)**, and move on.
- At the end, revisit all flagged essays in one sitting when you're fresh (e.g., Sunday morning). You'll resolve most of them quickly once removed from fatigue, and you can compare flagged essays *to each other*, which is easier than deciding in isolation.

### Step 5: Spot-check for reliability at the end
- Re-mark 5 essays you marked on Day 1, blind (cover your original marks).
- If your marks match within 1–2 points per criterion, you're reliably calibrated.
- If they don't, review your anchor set and re-skim essays marked in the affected session.

---

## Quick-Reference Card (print this, keep on desk)

| | 5 | 4 | 3 | 2 | 1/0 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Argument** | builds + rebuts | clear, logical | present but wobbly | absent/contradictory |
| **Evidence** | specific + developed | some support, thin | asserted, vague | none |
| **Structure** | intro/body/concl. flow | mechanical but present | disjointed | none |
| **Language** | fluent, accurate | minor errors | frequent errors | meaning lost |

---

## Practical Notes for the SA Grade 11 Context

- If your school/CAPS documentation requires a different total (e.g., out of 25 or aligned to a specific rubric format), the 4 criteria and level logic transfer directly — just rescale the marks per criterion.
- Keep the anchor set from this weekend. Reuse it (with new calibration essays added) for the next assignment — it will make Round 2 even faster.
- Consider photographing or keeping digital copies of your final anchor set with marks justified in 1–2 lines each. This becomes valuable evidence if a mark is ever queried by a parent or moderator.
